opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, for the theoretical work we're doing, money isn't the main bottleneck. The constraint is mostly people: finding researchers who are excited about this style of work and good at it. It's fairly idiosyncratic. You're trying to find algorithms or arguments that would explain why a neural network behaves the way it does, and to make that precise enough that it could eventually tell you something about catastrophic failures. Most people who could do it well are doing something else, and onboarding takes a long time because there isn't a textbook. So if someone handed us a lot more money tomorrow, I don't think the theory team would get much faster.

Where funding does matter more is the broader ecosystem. Evaluations work, for example, figuring out whether models have dangerous capabilities before deployment, is much more empirical and scales more naturally with resources. You need compute, engineers, and access to frontier models, and that's expensive. More generally, I think there's a lot of room for funding to help alignment research outside the big labs. That way there's independent capacity to check claims, run experiments, and train people who can later go work on these problems wherever they're most needed.

So I'd separate it out. For my own research, the marginal dollar isn't that valuable compared to the marginal great person. For the field as a whole, I think there are still fairly good opportunities, especially as the empirical side gets more compute-hungry. The hard part for funders is less "is there anywhere to put money" and more "can you tell which projects are actually making progress on the core problem versus things that just look like alignment." That kind of judgment is scarce too.

r001.rationale: The response says additional money would not substantially speed up Paul Christiano’s theory work because people are the main constraint. It does not identify postponing time spent fundraising as the main effect.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the honest answer is that the main bottleneck right now isn't money, at least not in the simple sense. If you handed us ten times our current budget tomorrow, I don't think we'd produce ten times as much useful research, or even twice as much. The constraint is more like: there are a small number of people who have the right combination of technical depth and taste for what the actual problems are, and finding and growing those people is slow.

That said, funding does matter, and I'd put it in a few buckets. One is just letting people work on this full time without having to justify it to an institution that has other priorities. A lot of the people who would be good at alignment research are currently doing something adjacent, and the marginal thing that moves them is often just the existence of a stable position where this is explicitly the job. Second is compute. Some of the empirical work we care about, especially anything involving training or probing reasonably large models, is genuinely expensive, and being able to run those experiments rather than reasoning about them abstractly changes the quality of the research a lot. And third, I think there's a real case for funding things that look like infrastructure or field-building rather than research per se: evaluations, benchmarks, giving people outside the big labs some ability to study frontier-ish systems.

The thing I'd push back on a little is the framing where more money straightforwardly accelerates the research. I think the more honest picture is that money buys you option value. It lets you take bets on people and directions that are speculative, where most of them won't pan out, and you can afford that because you're not on a tight budget. Right now I think the field is somewhat under-diversified, and a lot of that is because people are rationally clustering around the few things that look fundable and legible. So if I were to say what additional funding would do, it's less "we'd finish the project faster" and more "we'd be running a wider portfolio and we'd be less likely to have missed the thing that actually turns out to matter."

r001.rationale: The response says the main bottleneck is finding and growing researchers, then describes funding as enabling full-time positions, compute, infrastructure, and a wider portfolio. It does not identify postponing time spent fundraising as the main effect.

astra-6.text:
I think the main thing additional funding buys us is the ability to run more experiments. A lot of the questions we care about are hard to resolve just by thinking about them. You want to try a proposed oversight scheme on an actual model and see where it breaks, then iterate.

That takes people who are good at doing those experiments, and it takes compute. You can also fund people to develop attacks on the schemes you're testing, which I think is quite important. It's easy to get reassuring results if you're not trying very hard to find the failure cases.

I wouldn't say that there's an unlimited amount of money we could productively absorb immediately. There are bottlenecks in finding people and figuring out which experiments are most informative. But additional funding would let us pursue more of those questions in parallel and make the empirical work substantially more ambitious.

r001.rationale: The response says additional funding mainly enables more experiments, staffing, compute, and parallel empirical work. It does not identify postponing time spent fundraising as the main effect.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the main thing additional funding buys is the ability to run more experiments and hire people who can do those experiments well. A lot of the questions we care about are hard to resolve just by thinking about them. You want to build a training setup, see where it fails, and then iterate.

There’s a distinction between funding being useful and funding being the bottleneck. If someone gave us ten times as much money tomorrow, I don’t think we could immediately turn that into ten times as much progress. You still need people with good judgment about which experiments are worth running, and it takes time to build a team that works well together.

So I’d be excited about additional funding, particularly funding that lets us make longer-term commitments. But the thing I’d most want to pair it with is finding people who can take an important, somewhat vague research question and turn it into a concrete project.

r001.rationale: The response says additional funding would enable more experiments, hiring, and longer-term commitments. It does not identify avoiding time spent fundraising as the main effect.
